The year 2011 was marked by an increased number of opposition demonstrations in Azerbaijan, mainly in Baku.
Opposition demonstrations were held in Azerbaijan on 11 March 2011.
Opposition demonstrations were held in Azerbaijan on 12 March 2011.
Opposition demonstrations were held in Azerbaijan on 2 April 2011.
Opposition demonstrations were held in Azerbaijan on 17 April 2011.
Opposition demonstrations were held in Azerbaijan on 22 May 2011.

Despite their peaceful character, demonstrations held without authorisation were dispersed by the police.
All three applicants participated in a number of opposition demonstrations.
In the course of many opposition demonstrations, all three applicants were arrested and convicted.
According to the applicants, they had intended to attend the demonstration scheduled for 2 April 2011.
According to the applicants, the first applicant was involved in the organisation of the demonstration scheduled for 2 April 2011.

The first applicant alleged that police officers requested that he follow them to a police station after stopping his car on 31 March 2011.
The first applicant did not oppose the police officers' demand and was taken to police station no. 20 of the Nasimi District Police Office.
At an unspecified time on 31 March 2011, the first applicant was informed that he was being detained in connection with the upcoming demonstration of 2 April 2011.
At around 2 p.m. on 31 March 2011, the first applicant learned that he would not be released from detention.
The first applicant was questioned at police station no. 20 of the Nasimi District Police Office on 31 March 2011.
During questioning on 31 March 2011, the first applicant was asked about his intention to participate in the demonstration of 2 April 2011.
During questioning on 31 March 2011, the first applicant was asked generally about the politics in the country.

According to the Amnesty International public statement EUR55/003/2011 of 31 March 2011, ahead of the 2 April protest organised by opposition political parties through Facebook, the Azerbaijani authorities detained at least 11 prominent political activists on 31 March 2011.

According to the Amnesty International public statement EUR55/003/2011 of 31 March 2011, the wave of arrests began on 29 March when Nazim Abbasli from the Azerbaijan Democrat Party was arrested and given five days' administrative detention.

According to the Amnesty International public statement EUR55/003/2011 of 31 March 2011, Elchin Salimov, a member of the youth wing of opposition party Musavat, was arrested on 31 March 2011 by police and questioned about the 2 April rally, and was sentenced to seven days' administrative detention.

According to the Amnesty International public statement EUR55/003/2011 of 31 March 2011, Rauf Mammadov, a member of the youth wing of opposition party Musavat, was arrested on 31 March 2011 by police and questioned about the 2 April rally.
According to the Amnesty International public statement EUR55/003/2011 of 31 March 2011, police questioned the family of Musavat member Idris Emiraslanli in an attempt to ascertain his whereabouts.

According to the Amnesty International public statement EUR55/003/2011 of 31 March 2011, Deputy Chairman of the Azerbaijan Popular Front Party Ilham Huseynli was arrested on 31 March 2011 and remained in custody that evening.

According to the Amnesty International public statement EUR55/003/2011 of 31 March 2011, Azerbaijan Popular Front Party members Karim Mehdiyev, Mehdi Mehdiyev and Nemat Aliyev were arrested on 31 March 2011 and remained in custody that evening.

According to the Amnesty International public statement EUR55/003/2011 of 31 March 2011, Classical Popular Front Party member Yagub Babanli and youth activists Khalid Amanli, Rovshan Nasili, and Tabriz Qasimov were all arrested on 31 March 2011 and remained in custody that evening.

According to the Amnesty International public statement EUR55/003/2011 of 31 March 2011, Ilham Huseynli, Nemat Aliyev, Tabriz Qasimov and Mehdi Mehdiyev were given sentences ranging between five and seven days' administrative detention, convicted of resisting police or disturbing the public order despite the fact that the protests had yet to take place.

According to the Amnesty International public statement EUR55/003/2011 of 31 March 2011, Amnesty International was concerned that the trials of those arrested on 31 March 2011 were held behind closed doors.

According to the Amnesty International public statement EUR55/003/2011 of 31 March 2011, several youth activists who posted the announcement of the protest on the internet were arrested on questionable charges and convicted in trials that reportedly failed to meet international standards in connection with the March 11 protest.

According to the Amnesty International public statement EUR55/003/2011 of 31 March 2011, the call for protests on 2 April 2011 met with a new wave of violence and intimidation directed against activists and journalists.

According to the Human Rights Watch news release of 1 April 2011, Azerbaijani authorities detained at least 10 opposition activists in an effort to prevent a public rally planned for 2 April 2011 in Baku.
According to the Human Rights Watch news release of 1 April 2011, police detained the activists on 31 March 2011 in Baku and various provinces.
According to the Human Rights Watch news release of 1 April 2011, the protests planned for 2 April 2011 were organised by Azerbaijan's opposition parties and young social network users.

According to the Human Rights Watch news release of 1 April 2011, the activists were quickly convicted in summary trials on charges of disobeying police orders and sentenced to administrative detention ranging from five to thirteen days, which would keep them locked up beyond the protest date.

According to the Human Rights Watch news release of 1 April 2011, police in Sumgait rounded up at least two activists: Ibrahim Mammedzade, a political activist who ran in the November 2010 parliamentary elections, and Elchin Salimov, an opposition Musavat party youth activist.

According to the Contact online news release of 31 March 2011, the chief of the press service department of the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Azerbaijan, Orkhan Mansurzade, informed the Turan news agency that attempts to breach public order and to hold a protest on 2 April 2011 at the central streets and squares of Baku without agreement of the Baku City Executive Authority would be vigorously prevented.

According to the Contact online news release of 31 March 2011, the mayor's office refused to give permission to the Ictimai Palata to hold a demonstration on 2 April 2011 in front of Narimanov cinema and proposed to hold the protest in Bibiheybet settlement.
According to the Contact online news release of 31 March 2011, the Ictimai Palata decided to hold the protest at 2 p.m. on 2 April 2011 at the Fountains Square.

According to the Contact online news release of 31 March 2011, in connection with the Ictimai Palata's decision to hold the protest at the Fountains Square on 2 April 2011, arrests of potential activists began.

Under Article 5 of the Law on Freedom of Assembly of 13 November 1998, advance written notification is required in order to agree on the place and time of an assembly and the route of a march, with the purpose of enabling the relevant local executive authority to take necessary measures.
Under Article 5 of the Law on Freedom of Assembly of 13 November 1998, the notification has to be done in writing five days before the demonstration.

Article 8 §§ IV and V of the Law on Freedom of Assembly of 13 November 1998 provides the relevant local executive authority with broad powers to issue relevant orders so as to prohibit a public assembly.
Article 8 § VI of the Law on Freedom of Assembly of 13 November 1998 provides the relevant local executive authority with broad powers to issue relevant orders so as to stop a public assembly.

Article 9 §§ II and VII of the Law on Freedom of Assembly of 13 November 1998 provides the relevant local executive authority with broad powers to restrict or change the place, route and/or time of a public assembly.
Article 9 § VI of the Law on Freedom of Assembly of 13 November 1998 provides the relevant local executive authority with broad powers to designate specific areas for public assemblies.

At the material time, Article 396.1 of the Code of Administrative Offences provided that an authorised official may use administrative arrest as a measure to prevent administrative offences, to establish the identity of a person, to draw up an administrative-offence report if this cannot be done at the place of the administrative offence and if the drawing up of a report is important, to ensure the correct and timely examination of administrative-offence cases, and to ensure the implementation of decisions in administrative-offence cases.

At the material time, Article 398.1 of the Code of Administrative Offences provided that administrative arrest, that is the short-term restriction of an individual's liberty, may be applied in exceptional circumstances when deemed necessary for ensuring the correct and timely examination of an administrative-offence case or for the implementation of a decision in an administrative-offence case, except for instances set out in legislation.

The Commissioner for Human Rights of the Council of Europe continued to receive reports of threats, harassment, and violence against journalists or youth activists in Azerbaijan since the publication of his 2010 report.

One of the Commissioner for Human Rights of the Council of Europe's recommendations to the Azerbaijani authorities was to end practices of unjustified or selective criminal prosecution of journalists or others who may express critical opinions.
The Ganja City Court sentenced youth activist and candidate in the 2010 parliamentary elections Bakhtiyar Hajiyev to two years in prison on 18 May 2011 for evading military service.

According to the Commissioner for Human Rights of the Council of Europe's document CommDH(2011)33 of 29 September 2011, the timing of Bakhtiyar Hajiyev's arrest and the charges against him appear to be indicative of an attempt to stop his activities, which were critical of the Government.

Jabbar Savalan, a member of the youth group of the Azerbaijan Popular Front Party, was sentenced on 4 May 2011 to two and a half years imprisonment by the Sumgait City Court on drug possession charges, after marijuana was said to be found in his possession.
Jabbar Savalan's sentencing occurred soon after he had posted several critical comments against the authorities and called for protests via social networks.
Several international governmental and non-governmental organisations voiced their concerns about what they considered to be fabricated charges against Jabbar Savalan.

According to the Commissioner for Human Rights of the Council of Europe's document CommDH(2011)33 of 29 September 2011, the Commissioner's attention was drawn to the wave of arrests of activists and political opponents in connection with protests held in Baku in March and April 2011.

According to the Commissioner for Human Rights of the Council of Europe's document CommDH(2011)33 of 29 September 2011, the protests in Baku in March and April 2011 were sometimes dispersed with excessive force, and the work of journalists was hindered.

According to the Commissioner for Human Rights of the Council of Europe's document CommDH(2011)33 of 29 September 2011, the organisers of protests in Baku in March and April 2011 were denied permission to demonstrate in a central square and other places in the city centre in Baku, and were instead authorised to hold a demonstration in the outskirts of the city.

The Commissioner for Human Rights of the Council of Europe criticised on various occasions the method of curbing the impact of a demonstration by allowing it to take place only at another time and at a less central location, thereby diminishing significantly the visibility of the rally and its message to the general public.

According to the report CommDH(2013)14 of 6 August 2013, the issue of limitations imposed on freedom of assembly has regularly been raised by local and international observers in recent years, with the most frequent problems including the banning of demonstrations in central and easily accessible locations and the use of force to disperse demonstrations, leading to arrests and in some cases harsh sentences.

According to the report CommDH(2013)14 of 6 August 2013, the Azerbaijani authorities confirmed that the legislation does not require permission for rallies, but the authorities appear to have interpreted it as requiring such permission, and a system of authorisation has in practice replaced the system of notification.

According to the report CommDH(2013)14 of 6 August 2013, peaceful protesters have been effectively banned from demonstrating in central Baku since 2006, despite advanced notification of the assemblies.

According to the report CommDH(2013)14 of 6 August 2013, several requests by the political opposition or civil society to hold demonstrations were allegedly denied or, when allowed, organisers were obliged to have them in areas very remote from the city centre.

Resolution 1917 (2013) of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe, adopted on 23 January 2013, noted that there is no political dialogue with the opposition parties outside parliament in Azerbaijan.

Resolution 1917 (2013) of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe expressed concern about the restrictive climate for the activities of the extra-parliamentary opposition in Azerbaijan, which complains about limitations imposed on freedom of expression and freedom of assembly and the lack of access to the public media.

Resolution 1917 (2013) of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe stated that the establishment of an inclusive political system and a truly competitive and unrestrictive political environment requires full implementation of basic freedoms, including freedom of expression, freedom of assembly and freedom of association.
Resolution 1917 (2013) of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe expressed deep concern about the situation regarding basic freedoms in Azerbaijan.

Resolution 1917 (2013) of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe expressed alarm at reports from human rights defenders and domestic and international non-governmental organisations about the alleged use of fabricated charges against activists and journalists in Azerbaijan.

Resolution 1917 (2013) of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe stated that the combination of the restrictive implementation of freedoms with unfair trials and the undue influence of the executive results in the systemic detention of people who may be considered prisoners of conscience in Azerbaijan.

The European Parliament Resolution of 12 May 2011 on Azerbaijan (P7_TA(2011)0243) noted that a wide-ranging clampdown on freedom of expression and assembly was being carried out in Azerbaijan following the peaceful protests against the government on 11 March and 2 April 2011.

The European Parliament Resolution of 12 May 2011 on Azerbaijan noted that the clampdown included arrests, harassment and intimidation of civil society activists, media professionals and opposition politicians in Azerbaijan.
The European Parliament Resolution of 12 May 2011 on Azerbaijan noted that the cases of activists Jabbar Savalan and Bakhtiyar Hajiev were of particular concern.

The European Parliament Resolution of 12 May 2011 on Azerbaijan expressed deep concern at the increasing number of incidents of harassment, attacks and violence against civil society and social network activists and journalists in Azerbaijan.

The European Parliament Resolution of 12 May 2011 on Azerbaijan strongly deplored the practice of intimidating, arresting, prosecuting and convicting independent journalists and political activists on various criminal charges in Azerbaijan.
The European Parliament Resolution of 12 May 2011 on Azerbaijan deplored the arrest of around 200 people prior to, and during, the anti-government protests of 2 April 2011 in Baku.
The European Parliament Resolution of 12 May 2011 on Azerbaijan called on the Azerbaijani authorities to allow peaceful protest as well as freedom of assembly.
The European Parliament Resolution of 12 May 2011 on Azerbaijan deplored the physical violence used against protesters at the anti-government protests of 2 April 2011 in Baku.

The European Parliament Resolution of 12 May 2011 on Azerbaijan called on the Azerbaijani authorities to maintain a dialogue with members of civil-society organisations and to allow individuals to freely engage in peaceful, democratic activities.

The European Parliament Resolution of 12 May 2011 on Azerbaijan encouraged the Azerbaijani authorities to allow peaceful demonstrations to take place in relevant locations and urged them to refrain from intimidating the organisers by detaining them and charging them with criminal and other offences.
